claim: C. elegans was the first organism for which a full nervous system connectome was established.
source: The nematode Caenorhabditis elegans was the first organism for which a full nervous system connectome was established (White et al., 1986).
evidence: Supported by citation to White et al., 1986

claim: Connectomes exist for both sexes of C. elegans.
source: Connectomes now exist for both sexes (Cook et al., 2019; Hall and Russell, 1991; White et al., 1986)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cook et al., 2019; Hall and Russell, 1991; White et al., 1986

claim: Connectomes exist for the C. elegans pharynx.
source: Connectomes now exist for both sexes (Cook et al., 2019; Hall and Russell, 1991; White et al., 1986), the pharynx (Cook et al., 2020; Albertson and Thomson, 1976)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cook et al., 2020; Albertson and Thomson, 1976

claim: Connectomes exist for different developmental stages of C. elegans.
source: Connectomes now exist for both sexes (Cook et al., 2019; Hall and Russell, 1991; White et al., 1986), the pharynx (Cook et al., 2020; Albertson and Thomson, 1976), for different developmental stages (Brittin et al., 2021; Witvliet et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Brittin et al., 2021; Witvliet et al., 2021

claim: A connectome exists for the C. elegans dauer diapause stage.
source: Connectomes now exist for both sexes (Cook et al., 2019; Hall and Russell, 1991; White et al., 1986), the pharynx (Cook et al., 2020; Albertson and Thomson, 1976), for different developmental stages (Brittin et al., 2021; Witvliet et al., 2021), and for the dauer diapause stage (Yim et al., 2023).
evidence: Supported by citation to Yim et al., 2023

claim: Understanding of developmental and inter-individual variability in synaptic connectivity in C. elegans is only beginning.
source: For example, we are only beginning to understand the extent of developmental and inter-individual variability in synaptic connectivity and adjacency (Cook et al., 2023; Brittin et al., 2021; Witvliet et al., 2021)
evidence: Supported by citations to Cook et al., 2023; Brittin et al., 2021; Witvliet et al., 2021

claim: How external or internal factors establish, alter, and maintain the synaptic connectome in C. elegans remains largely unknown.
source: but we remain much in the dark of how exactly external or internal factors establish, alter, and maintain the synaptic connectome.
evidence: Statement of current knowledge gap

claim: A lack of synaptic fluorescent reporters and difficulty in scoring them remain a bottleneck for large-scale mutant analyses in C. elegans.
source: a lack of synaptic fluorescent reporters and difficulty in scoring them remain a bottleneck for large-scale mutant analyses.
evidence: Statement of current limitations in the field

claim: The nerve ring is a synapse-dense region of the C. elegans nervous system.
source: This is especially true in the synapse-dense regions of the C. elegans nervous system, such as the nerve ring.
evidence: Statement based on established anatomical knowledge

claim: Chemical synapses in C. elegans can be visualized using fluorescently tagged presynaptic proteins such as SNB-1/VAMP, RAB-3, SYD-2/Liprin, and CLA-1/Piccolo.
source: For chemical synapses, these include reporters labeling pre- and post-synaptic proteins – such as SNB-1/VAMP, RAB-3, SYD-2/Liprin, CLA-1/Piccolo, and GLR-1/AMPAR – fused with a fluorescent protein (Xuan et al., 2017; Mahoney et al., 2006; Yeh et al., 2005; Shen and Bargmann, 2003; Zhen and Jin, 1999; Nonet, 1999; Rongo et al., 1998; Jorgensen et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published work

claim: GRASP is a split-fluorophore transsynaptic technology used to visualize chemical synapses in C. elegans.
source: and split-fluorophore transsynaptic technology such as GFP Reconstitution Across Synaptic Partners (GRASP) (Feinberg et al., 2008) and other variants (Feng et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2019)
evidence: Supported by citations to Feinberg et al., 2008; Feng et al., 2020; Feng et al., 2019

claim: iBLINC is a transsynaptic technology used to visualize chemical synapses in C. elegans.
source: and Biotin Labeling of Intercellular Contacts (iBLINC) (Desbois et al., 2015; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citation to Desbois et al., 2015

claim: Innexins can be endogenously tagged with fluorescent proteins to visualize electrical synapses in C. elegans.
source: In the case of electrical synapses, innexins can be endogenously tagged with fluorescent proteins to visualize homo- or heteromeric electrical synapses (Hendi et al., 2022; Gordon et al., 2020; Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hendi et al., 2022; Gordon et al., 2020; Bhattacharya et al., 2019

claim: CRISPR/Cas9 has made it easier to label endogenous genetic loci with fluorophores in C. elegans.
source: Moreover, the relative ease of labeling endogenous genetic loci with a fluorophore using CRISPR/Cas9 (Eroglu et al., 2023; Ghanta et al., 2021; Ghanta and Mello, 2020) has led to an increase in reporters with fluorophore-tagged proteins localized at chemical and electrical synapses (Zhou et al., 2021; Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Lipton et al., 2018; Tu et al., 2015; Pinan-Lucarré et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by citations to CRISPR/Cas9 methods and resulting reporters

claim: Synaptic reporters have been instrumental in studying synaptogenesis in C. elegans.
source: These reporters have been instrumental in studying synapse biology in abundant paradigms including, but not restricted to, synaptogenesis (Mizumoto et al., 2023; Kurshan and Shen, 2019; Jin, 2005)
evidence: Supported by citations to Mizumoto et al., 2023; Kurshan and Shen, 2019; Jin, 2005

claim: Synaptic reporters have been instrumental in studying sexual dimorphism in C. elegans.
source: These reporters have been instrumental in studying synapse biology in abundant paradigms including, but not restricted to, synaptogenesis (Mizumoto et al., 2023; Kurshan and Shen, 2019; Jin, 2005), sexual dimorphism (Pechuk et al., 2022; Salzberg et al., 2020; Bayer et al., 2020; Bayer and Hobert, 2018; Cook et al., 2019; Hart and Hobert, 2018; Weinberg et al., 2018; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016)
evidence: Supported by citations to multiple studies on sexual dimorphism

claim: Synaptic reporters have been instrumental in studying experience-dependent plasticity in C. elegans.
source: These reporters have been instrumental in studying synapse biology in abundant paradigms including, but not restricted to, synaptogenesis (Mizumoto et al., 2023; Kurshan and Shen, 2019; Jin, 2005), sexual dimorphism (Pechuk et al., 2022; Salzberg et al., 2020; Bayer et al., 2020; Bayer and Hobert, 2018; Cook et al., 2019; Hart and Hobert, 2018; Weinberg et al., 2018; Oren-Suissa et al., 2016), and experience-dependent plasticity (Chandra et al., 2023; Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Bayer and Hobert, 2018; Hart and Hobert, 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Chandra et al., 2023; Bhattacharya et al., 2019; Bayer and Hobert, 2018; Hart and Hobert, 2018

claim: This paper presents a toolkit of novel synaptic reporters for the C. elegans community.
source: A toolkit of novel reporters is presented in this paper as a resource for the C. elegans community (Figure 1B, Supplementary file 1).
evidence: Direct statement about the paper's contribution, with reference to figures and supplementary materials

claim: WormPsyQi is a generalizable image analysis pipeline that automatically quantifies synaptically localized fluorescent signals.
source: In this paper, we describe WormPsyQi, a generalizable image analysis pipeline that automatically quantifies synaptically localized fluorescent signals in a high-throughput and robust manner, with reduced human bias.
evidence: Direct description of the pipeline developed in this study

claim: This paper presents 30 transgenic strains that label chemical or electrical synapses throughout the C. elegans nervous system.
source: We also present a resource of 30 transgenic strains that label chemical or electrical synapses throughout the nervous system of the nematode Caenorhabditis elegans, using CLA-1, RAB-3, GRASP (chemical synapses), or innexin (electrical synapse) reporters.
evidence: Direct statement about the resource provided in this paper

claim: WormPsyQi captures synaptic structures despite substantial heterogeneity in neurite morphology, fluorescence signal, and imaging parameters.
source: We show that WormPsyQi captures synaptic structures in spite of substantial heterogeneity in neurite morphology, fluorescence signal, and imaging parameters.
evidence: Statement of the pipeline's capabilities demonstrated in the study

claim: WormPsyQi can quantify multiple features of synapses including number, size, intensity, and spatial distribution.
source: We use these toolkits to quantify multiple obvious and subtle features of synapses – such as number, size, intensity, and spatial distribution of synapses – in datasets spanning various regions of the nervous system, developmental stages, and sexes.
evidence: Description of the pipeline's quantification capabilities demonstrated in the study

claim: The WormPsyQi pipeline may be utilized for other 'punctate' signals beyond synapses.
source: Although the pipeline is described in the context of synapses, it may be utilized for other 'punctate' signals, such as fluorescently tagged neurotransmitter receptors and cell adhesion molecules, as well as proteins in other subcellular contexts.
evidence: Statement about potential broader applications of the pipeline

claim: Manual synaptic puncta quantification in large image datasets is tedious and low in throughput.
source: Manual synaptic puncta quantification in large image datasets can be problematic (San-Miguel et al., 2016; Crane et al., 2012). Firstly, it is tedious and low in throughput
evidence: Statement about limitations of manual quantification, supported by citations

claim: Manual quantification of synapses in neurons with high synapse density and complex neurite morphologies can take up to several hours.
source: for neurons with high synapse density and complex neurite morphologies in three-dimensional (3D) space, it can take up to several hours to quantify a dataset of typical size.
evidence: Statement based on practical experience with manual quantification

claim: Manual quantification requires a priori information about the region of interest.
source: Secondly, manual quantification requires some a priori information about the region of interest (ROI), thus discouraging observation outside the ROI that may be of relevance in different genetic conditions or environmental backgrounds.
evidence: Statement about limitations of manual quantification approach

claim: Manual quantification introduces human error and bias in cases where the fluorescent signal is dim, synapse density is high, the SNR is poor, and neurons have complex morphologies.
source: Lastly, manual quantification introduces human error and bias in cases where the fluorescent signal is dim, synapse density is high, the SNR is poor, and neurons have complex morphologies that obstruct manual counting in a 3D image stack.
evidence: Statement about limitations of manual quantification

claim: WormPsyQi consists of five key steps: neurite mask segmentation, synapse segmentation, validation and correction, re-labeling and training, and quantification.
source: WormPsyQi consists of five key steps: neurite mask segmentation (optional), synapse segmentation, validation and correction, re-labeling and training (optional), and quantification (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Description of the pipeline structure with reference to figure

claim: WormPsyQi uses a modified U-Net convolutional neural network architecture for neurite segmentation.
source: For neurite segmentation, we modified a convolutional neural network architecture, U-Net (Guo et al., 2022; Guo et al., 2020; Ronneberger et al., 2015), to robustly segment the neurite and soma, and create a mask that helps in specifying the ROI in which synapses are later segmented (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Description of the method used, with citations to U-Net architecture

claim: Masking prior to synapse segmentation is critical if the signal-to-noise ratio is poor.
source: Masking prior to synapse segmentation is critical if the SNR is poor; it also significantly reduces the overall image processing time by constraining synapse segmentation within the neurite mask.
evidence: Statement about the importance of masking step based on pipeline performance

claim: WormPsyQi provides four pre-trained default models optimized to detect different types of synapses.
source: Image datasets from four diverse synaptic reporters were used to train four independent default models optimized to detect (1) small synapses (1–3 pixels radius) with low SNR (e.g. puncta with similar intensity and morphology as autofluorescence noise in surrounding tissue), (2) small synapses with high SNR, (3) medium-sized synapses (3–10 pixels radius), and (4) diffuse (>10 pixels radius) signal (see Methods for more detail).
evidence: Description of the pre-trained models provided with the pipeline

claim: A minimum of one fully labeled image in the training set is sufficient for WormPsyQi's segmentation accuracy to converge.
source: In our experience, a minimum of one fully labeled image stack in the training set is sufficient for the segmentation accuracy to converge (Figure 2C).
evidence: Statement based on experimental results shown in Figure 2C

claim: The IoU score between WormPsyQi's segmentation and the original labeler's annotation was significantly higher than the inter-expert IoU.
source: Notably, the IoU between WormPsyQi's segmentation and the original labeler's annotation was significantly higher than the inter-expert IoU (Figure 2D, columns 2 and 3), indicating that WormPsyQi allows standardized quantification of synaptic features, which human annotators cannot.
evidence: Statement of results from validation experiment shown in Figure 2D

claim: WormPsyQi achieves over a 10-fold reduction in processing time compared to manual annotation.
source: (E) WormPsyQi achieves over a 10-fold reduction in processing time: while labelers 1 and 2 took 130 and 160 min to annotate puncta, respectively, WormPsyQi processed the same dataset (15 images) in 13 min using an affordable desktop machine.
evidence: Quantitative comparison of processing times shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 4E

claim: WormPsyQi validates sex-specific synapses in adult hermaphrodites and males.
source: WormPsyQi validates sex-specific synapses in adult hermaphrodites and males.
evidence: Statement of validation results, with data shown in Figure 3

claim: PHB>AVA synapses are sexually dimorphic, with fewer synapses in adult males compared to hermaphrodites.
source: We show here that WormPsyQi reliably validates previous observations: synapses between ADL>AVA, PHB>AVA, and PHA>AVG are sexually dimorphic, such that synapse number in adult males is less compared to hermaphrodites
evidence: Statement of results validated by WormPsyQi, consistent with previous EM data

claim: PHA>AVG synapses are sexually dimorphic, with fewer synapses in adult males compared to hermaphrodites.
source: We show here that WormPsyQi reliably validates previous observations: synapses between ADL>AVA, PHB>AVA, and PHA>AVG are sexually dimorphic, such that synapse number in adult males is less compared to hermaphrodites
evidence: Statement of results validated by WormPsyQi, consistent with previous EM data

claim: ADL>AVA synapses are sexually dimorphic, with fewer synapses in adult males compared to hermaphrodites.
source: We show here that WormPsyQi reliably validates previous observations: synapses between ADL>AVA, PHB>AVA, and PHA>AVG are sexually dimorphic, such that synapse number in adult males is less compared to hermaphrodites
evidence: Statement of results validated by WormPsyQi, consistent with previous EM data

claim: PHB>AVG synapses are sexually dimorphic, with fewer synapses in adult hermaphrodites compared to males.
source: and PHB>AVG synapses are less in adult hermaphrodites compared to males (Figure 3B–E).
evidence: Statement of results validated by WormPsyQi, with data shown in Figure 3

claim: Cell-specific RAB-3 reporters have a more diffuse synaptic signal compared to CLA-1 reporters for the same neuron.
source: For instance, cell-specific RAB-3 reporters have a more diffuse synaptic signal compared to the punctate signal in CLA-1 reporters for the same neuron, as shown for the neuron pair ASK (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C) and observed previously in other neurons (Cook et al., 2020; Lipton et al., 2018; Xuan et al., 2017).
evidence: Observation from data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C, supported by citations to previous observations

claim: The difference in signal between RAB-3 and CLA-1 reporters is due to the distinct localization and function of RAB-3 and CLA-1.
source: This is intuitive based on the distinct localization and function of RAB-3, a presynaptic vesicle protein (Nonet et al., 1997), and CLA-1/Piccolo, an active zone scaffolding protein that recruits synapse vesicles to release sites (Xuan et al., 2017).
evidence: Explanation based on known protein functions, supported by citations

claim: WormPsyQi is unable to reliably segment puncta in synapse-dense neurons such as AIB and SAA using RAB-3 reporters.
source: While this may not be a problem for neurons or regions with low synapse density (e.g. ASK RAB-3 and CLA-1 puncta number are similar as shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C), it poses challenges for synapse-dense cases such as AIB and SAA, where WormPsyQi is unable to reliably segment puncta using any of the four pre-trained models.
evidence: Statement of pipeline limitations based on testing with different reporters

claim: Fluorescent signals from GRASP and iBLINC reporters vary across neurons or synapses.
source: Fluorescent signals from GRASP and iBLINC reporters appear different from other reporters and is wide-ranging across neurons or synapses (Figure 5).
evidence: Observation from data shown in Figure 5

claim: Variability in GRASP and iBLINC signals is likely due to sensitivity to promoter choice, amount of injected DNA, transgene type, and imaging conditions.
source: As previously reported, this is likely due to transsynaptic labeling methods being more sensitive to the choice of promoters used to drive split-fluorophore fragments, amount of injected reporter DNA, extrachromosomal vs. integrated nature of transgenes, and imaging conditions (Oren-Suissa et al., 2016).
evidence: Explanation based on previous reports, supported by citation

claim: In most datasets, the difference between WormPsyQi and human annotation was statistically insignificant.
source: To confirm that WormPsyQi quantified fluorescent puncta accurately, we compared its results with manual quantification for a subset of reporters analyzed and found that in most datasets, the difference between WormPsyQi and human annotation was statistically insignificant (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, Figure 5).
evidence: Statement of validation results comparing WormPsyQi to manual quantification

claim: Having a cytoplasmic reporter in the background of the synaptic reporter enhanced WormPsyQi performance.
source: Generally, having a cytoplasmic reporter in the background of the synaptic reporter enhanced performance; it was also a crucial step in preventing synapse mis-annotation in regions with high background fluorescence intensity such as the tail, where adjacent intestinal autofluorescence typically masks bona fide synaptic signal.
evidence: Statement based on comparison of pipeline performance with and without cytoplasmic markers

claim: CLA-1 reporters are overall a superior marker compared to RAB-3 reporters for the same neuron.
source: We also found that CLA-1 reporters were overall a superior marker compared to RAB-3 reporters for the same neuron, as shown for ASK (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, C).
evidence: Comparative assessment based on data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claim: The C. elegans pharynx constitutes 14 neuron classes.
source: The C. elegans pharynx constitutes 14 neuron classes, and like the ENS in other organisms (Brehmer, 2021; Furness, 2007; Costa et al., 2000), there is substantial morphological heterogeneity among these neuron classes (Albertson and Thomson, 1976).
evidence: Statement of anatomical fact, supported by citations

claim: There is substantial morphological heterogeneity among pharyngeal neuron classes in C. elegans.
source: The C. elegans pharynx constitutes 14 neuron classes, and like the ENS in other organisms (Brehmer, 2021; Furness, 2007; Costa et al., 2000), there is substantial morphological heterogeneity among these neuron classes (Albertson and Thomson, 1976).
evidence: Statement supported by citations to anatomical studies

claim: Some pharyngeal neurons show variability in branching and synapses both within a bilateral pair and across individuals.
source: In addition, some neurons show variability in branching and synapses, both within a bilateral pair and across individuals, such as in the case of M3 L/R pair (Albertson and Thomson, 1976).
evidence: Statement supported by citation to Albertson and Thomson, 1976

claim: WormPsyQi can robustly segment pharyngeal neurites and generally performs well in quantifying synapses.
source: Our analyses show that WormPsyQi can robustly segment pharyngeal neurites and generally performs well in quantifying synapses, as with the CNS.
evidence: Statement of results from analysis of pharyngeal neurons

claim: In reporters for neurons I5, MC, NSM, and I2, there was no significant difference between puncta count measured by WormPsyQi vs. a human annotator.
source: This is shown by the comparison between manual and WormPsyQi counts for each reporter (Figure 6A–F). In reporters for neurons I5, MC, NSM, and I2, we found no significant difference between puncta count measured by the pipeline vs. a human annotator (Figure 6A–D).
evidence: Statement of validation results shown in Figure 6

claim: INX-6::GFP puncta are observed in the pharynx and the nerve ring.
source: INX-6::GFP (ot805) puncta are observed in the pharynx and the nerve ring.
evidence: Observation from imaging data shown in Figure 7

claim: INX-6 puncta in the nerve ring are significantly higher in dauer animals compared to L4 animals.
source: Given that outside of the pharynx, inx-6 is exclusively expressed in AIB interneurons in dauers, the puncta can be assigned to AIB axons as shown previously (Bhattacharya et al., 2019); in the absence of a cytoplasmic marker, WormPsyQi scores a limited number of puncta in L4 animals, but the dauer count significantly exceeds L4 count, as expected.
evidence: Statement of results consistent with previous findings, supported by citation

claim: Total ASK axon length in the nerve ring increases approximately twofold between late-L1 and adulthood.
source: Total ASK axon length in the nerve ring increases ~twofold between late-L1 and adulthood.
evidence: Quantitative measurement shown in Figure 8A

claim: The number of ASK presynaptic specializations increases approximately twofold between late-L1 and adulthood, in proportion with the increase in axon length.
source: The number of puncta increases ~twofold, which is in proportion with the increase in axon length across development.
evidence: Quantitative measurement and comparison shown in Figure 8B

claim: Neurons in the CNS progressively add synapses at pre-existing sites throughout larval development up until adulthood.
source: From our analysis, we found that generally neurons in the CNS progressively add synapses at pre-existing sites throughout larval development up until adulthood (Figure 8B–E).
evidence: General conclusion from developmental analysis shown in Figure 8

claim: System-wide neurite length in the nerve ring increases with the length of the animal.
source: In a previous study, a comparative analysis of the nerve ring from EM samples spanning multiple larval- and adult-staged C. elegans showed that system-wide neurite length increases with the length of the animal and that synapses are added progressively, thereby maintaining overall synapse density (Witvliet et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement based on previous EM study, supported by citation

claim: Synapses are added progressively during development, maintaining overall synapse density in the nerve ring.
source: In a previous study, a comparative analysis of the nerve ring from EM samples spanning multiple larval- and adult-staged C. elegans showed that system-wide neurite length increases with the length of the animal and that synapses are added progressively, thereby maintaining overall synapse density (Witvliet et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement based on previous EM study, supported by citation

claim: The length of the pharynx increases twofold between L1 and adulthood.
source: The length of the pharynx from the tip of the corpus to the end of the terminal bulb increases twofold (from 60 to 130 μm, roughly) between L1 and adulthood (Shibata et al., 2016).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from previous study, supported by citation

claim: The overall length of the C. elegans animal increases approximately 4.5-fold between L1 and adulthood.
source: This elongation is modest relative to the overall ~4.5-fold increase (from 250 to 1150 μm, roughly) in the length of the animal across the same developmental window (Witvliet et al., 2021; Shibata et al., 2016; Figure 9A).
evidence: Quantitative measurement from previous studies, supported by citations

claim: Neurons in the ENS show striking disparity in synapse addition across neuron classes.
source: We found that in contrast to neurons in the CNS, neurons in the ENS show striking disparity in synapse addition across neuron classes.
evidence: General conclusion from developmental analysis of pharyngeal neurons

claim: The number of CLA-1/RAB-3 puncta in neurons MC, I2, and M3 remains constant or increases modestly compared to the elongation of the pharynx between early larval stages and adulthood.
source: The number of CLA-1/RAB-3 puncta in neurons MC, I2, and M3 remains constant (neurons MC and I2, Figure 9B, C; Figure 9—figure supplement 1A, D) or increases modestly compared to the elongation of the pharynx (neuron M3, Figure 9D; Figure 9—figure supplement 1B) between early larval stages (L1 or L2) and adulthood.
evidence: Quantitative results shown in Figure 9 and supplementary figures

claim: Synapse density in pharyngeal neurons MC, I2, and M3 decreases across development.
source: In other words, synapse density in these neurons decreases across development.
evidence: Inference from the observation that synapse number does not scale with neurite length

claim: In neurons M4 and NSM, CLA-1/RAB-3 puncta are added proportionately with increasing neurite length and overall pharynx elongation across development.
source: In contrast to neurons that show variable synapse density across developmental stages, we found two neuron classes, M4 and NSM, where CLA-1/RAB-3 puncta are added proportionately with increasing neurite length and overall pharynx elongation across development ('Total count' in Figure 9E, F; Figure 9—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: Quantitative results shown in Figure 9

claim: M4 and NSM puncta largely correspond to neuromuscular junctions, many of which arise post-embryonically.
source: Based on previous EM studies (Cook et al., 2020; Albertson and Thomson, 1976), these puncta largely correspond to neuromuscular junctions, many of which arise post-embryonically and can be considered somewhat separate from the 'core' pharyngeal connectome established in the embryo which seems more static.
evidence: Interpretation based on previous EM studies, supported by citations

claim: Developmental synapse addition appears to differ between the ENS and CNS.
source: In conclusion, developmental synapse addition appears to differ between the ENS and CNS, as suggested by the lesser increase in synapse number in pharyngeal neurons relative to somatic neurons in our data (Figures 8 and 9).
evidence: Comparative conclusion from developmental analyses shown in Figures 8 and 9

claim: In PHA neurons, presynaptic sites are concentrated and uniformly distributed in the axonal region anterior to the branch point with close to no synapse posterior to it.
source: Previous EM data (Cook et al., 2019; White et al., 1986) show that in PHA neurons, presynaptic sites are concentrated – and uniformly distributed – in the axonal region anterior to the branch point with close to no synapse posterior to it; our PHA-specific RAB-3 reporter recapitulates this topological distribution (Figure 10A).
evidence: Comparison of reporter data with previous EM data, supported by citations

claim: AIB's axons occupy two distinct neighborhoods of the nerve ring, anterior and posterior, with a majority of presynaptic sites localizing in the anterior region.
source: AIB's axons occupy two distinct neighborhoods of the nerve ring (Moyle et al., 2021), anterior and posterior, with a majority of presynaptic sites localizing in the anterior region (Sengupta et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement based on previous studies, supported by citations

claim: In AIB neurons, synapse density is sparse in the ventral regions but increases gradually as the processes travel to the crossover point at the dorsal midline, with highest density proximal to it.
source: Quantification of topological synapse distribution within the anterior axon in a representative population revealed that synapse density is sparse in the ventral regions, but increases gradually as the processes travel to the crossover point at the dorsal midline, with highest density proximal to it.
evidence: Quantitative analysis of spatial distribution shown in Figure 10B

claim: The total volume of synapses in ASK neurons scaled proportionately with synapse addition between L1 and adult animals.
source: The total volume of synapses scaled proportionately with synapse addition between L1 and adult animals (Figure 10D)
evidence: Quantitative analysis shown in Figure 10D

claim: Peaks in probability density of synapse distribution in ASK neurons were stereotyped across development.
source: and peaks in probability density were stereotyped as well (Figure 10E), suggesting that these ultrastructure and spatial quantifications followed the same extent of plasticity as the overall number of synapses did.
evidence: Analysis of spatial distribution shown in Figure 10E

claim: The overall architecture of the brain in terms of cell body positions, neuronal morphologies, and relative arrangement of processes within neighborhoods in C. elegans are largely maintained across development.
source: Although this analysis is limited to a few neurons, the observation that synapse distribution – for synapses that are present at birth – remains stereotyped is not unanticipated given that, aside from inter-individual variability, the overall architecture of the brain in terms of cell body positions, neuronal morphologies, and relative arrangement of processes within neighborhoods in C. elegans are largely maintained across development (Witvliet et al., 2021; Moyle et al., 2021; Brittin et al., 2021).
evidence: Statement based on previous studies, supported by citations

claim: The reporters presented contain over-expressed multicopy transgenic arrays, which could lead to trafficking and localization artifacts.
source: Another limitation of the reporters described is that they contain over-expressed multicopy transgenic arrays, which could lead to trafficking and localization artifacts.
evidence: Statement of potential limitation of the transgenic approach

claim: Comparisons of multiple reporters expressing an identical transgene often show variability across lines picked from the same injection.
source: Comparisons of multiple reporters expressing an identical transgene often show variability across lines picked from the same injection.
evidence: Observation from experience with transgenic reporters

claim: Variability in GRASP and iBLINC reporters could partially explain discrepancies between data from transgenic reporters and EM reconstructions.
source: This could partially explain discrepancies between data from transgenic reporters and EM reconstructions (Figures 5, 6, 8).
evidence: Inference about potential source of discrepancies observed in the data

claim: Reporters with endogenously tagged proteins and single-copy transgenes show more consistent expression and spatial localization.
source: Reporters with endogenously tagged proteins and single-copy transgenes show more consistent expression and spatial localization.
evidence: Statement based on general knowledge of transgenic approaches

claim: WormPsyQi is constrained by the type of images and reporters being analyzed.
source: Lastly, although we have shown that the image analysis pipeline is robust and versatile, it is constrained by the type of images and reporters being analyzed.
evidence: Statement of pipeline limitations

claim: Where the synapse signal is diffuse or synapse density is too high, WormPsyQi quantification can be inaccurate.
source: Also, where the synapse signal is diffuse (e.g. RAB-3 reporters) or synapse density is too high (e.g. CLA-1/RAB-3 reporters for IL2, NSM, AIB, etc., Figures 4 and 6), quantification can be inaccurate.
evidence: Statement of pipeline limitations based on testing with various reporters

claim: If the fluorescent signal in an image is visibly discrete, WormPsyQi works well in quantifying many discernible and subtle features.
source: In general, if the fluorescent signal in an image is visibly discrete, WormPsyQi works well in quantifying many discernible and subtle features that would otherwise be tedious or impossible to achieve.
evidence: General conclusion about pipeline performance based on testing

claim: Wild-type strains used were C. elegans Bristol (strain N2).
source: Wild-type strains used were C. elegans Bristol (strain N2).
evidence: Statement of materials used in the study

claim: Worms were grown at 20°C on nematode growth media plates seeded with E. coli OP50.
source: Worms were grown at 20°C on nematode growth media plates seeded with bacteria (E. coli OP50).
evidence: Statement of methods used in the study

claim: Transgenic strains were generated by microinjecting constructs as simple extrachromosomal arrays into N2 or him-5 (e1490) genetic backgrounds.
source: Transgenic strains were generated by microinjecting constructs as simple extrachromosomal arrays into N2 or him-5 (e1490) genetic backgrounds.
evidence: Statement of methods used to generate transgenic strains

claim: Worms were anesthetized using 100 mM sodium azide (NaN3) for microscopy.
source: Worms were anesthetized using 100 mM sodium azide (NaN3) and mounted on 5% agar on glass slides.
evidence: Statement of methods used for imaging

claim: The resolution of the confocal microscope used for GFP imaging was estimated to be approximately 250 nm.
source: When using GFP, we estimated the resolution of our confocal to be ~250 nm.
